Once there is a search, the general rule is that it needs a warrant: issued by a neutral judge, based on probable cause (a fair probability that evidence of a crime will be found, judged by the totality of the circumstances, Illinois v. Gates, 1983), and particularly describing what is to be searched. But the Court has recognized many exceptions, and in practice most searches are warrantless.

head: Exception
Leading case
What it allows
rows: a search a person voluntarily agrees to; knowing of the right to refuse is not required
seizing evidence in plain view from a lawful vantage point, if its incriminating nature is immediately apparent
searching the arrested person and the area within his immediate control; not a whole house. Cell phone data needs a warrant (Riley v. California (2014))
searching a car with probable cause, because cars can be moved quickly
emergencies: hot pursuit, preventing evidence destruction, helping someone in danger
a brief stop on reasonable suspicion of crime; a pat-down for weapons if the person may be armed and dangerous

opts.facts: A Cleveland detective watched two men walk back and forth past a store window many times, peering in, and confer with a third man. Suspecting a robbery, he stopped them, patted down their outer clothing and found guns.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Warren wrote that a stop and frisk is a seizure and a search, but a limited one. An officer may briefly stop a person when he has reasonable suspicion, based on specific and articulable facts, that crime is afoot; he may pat down outer clothing if he reasonably believes the person is armed and dangerous.
opts.dissent: Justice Douglas dissented, arguing that the police were given more power than a judge would have to issue a warrant, which requires probable cause.

blocks.html: The standards form a ladder. Reasonable suspicion (for a Terry stop) is less than probable cause (for an arrest, a warrant or the automobile exception), which is less than proof at trial. Each step up allows a greater intrusion. Exceptions have limits that track their reasons. A search incident to arrest protects officers and preserves evidence, so it reaches only what the arrested person could grab; in Riley v. California (2014) the Court held that the digital contents of a phone pose neither danger, so police generally need a warrant: in the Chief Justice's words, "get a warrant."

Searches generally need a warrant on probable cause. Exceptions: consent, plain view, search incident to arrest (Chimel v. California (1969)), the automobile exception (Carroll v. United States (1925)), exigent circumstances, and stop and frisk on reasonable suspicion (Terry v. Ohio (1968)).

blocks.title: A traffic stop
blocks.q: Police stop a car for speeding. An officer smells what he reasonably identifies as burning marijuana, in a state where it is illegal, and searches the trunk. Which exception, and is it satisfied?
steps: The odor gives probable cause to believe the car holds evidence of a crime.
Under the automobile exception (Carroll), police may search a car, including its trunk and containers, with probable cause and no warrant.
blocks.a: Automobile exception; satisfied by probable cause.

blocks.title: After an arrest at home
blocks.q: Officers arrest a suspect in his living room, then search every room of the house without a warrant. Valid?
steps: Chimel limits a search incident to arrest to the person and the area within his immediate control.
Other rooms are beyond that area (a quick "protective sweep" for dangerous people is a separate, narrower rule).
blocks.a: No; searching the whole house exceeds Chimel.

blocks.html: Confusing probable cause with reasonable suspicion. Reasonable suspicion (for a Terry stop and frisk) is a lower standard than probable cause (for an arrest, a warrant or a car search). Check which intrusion is being justified.

If police violate the Fourth Amendment, what happens? The amendment does not say. The Court's main remedy is the exclusionary rule: evidence obtained through an unconstitutional search or seizure generally may not be used at trial to prove guilt.

blocks.name: cv-timeline
blocks.cap: The exclusionary rule and its exceptions.

opts.facts: In 1957 Cleveland police forced their way into Dollree Mapp's home looking for a bombing suspect, waving a paper they claimed was a warrant (none was ever produced). They found no suspect but seized materials they said were obscene, and she was convicted for possessing them.
opts.reasoning: Justice Clark wrote that the exclusionary rule is an essential part of the Fourth Amendment right, and that without it the right is "a form of words." Wolf v. Colorado (1949) had applied the right to the states but not the remedy; Mapp applied both.

blocks.html: Why exclude reliable evidence? Supporters say it is the only effective deterrent to unlawful searches and keeps courts from taking part in violations. Critics, in Justice Cardozo's famous line from his time on New York's court, say "the criminal is to go free because the constable has blundered." Since the 1970s the Court has treated the rule as a deterrent, applied only where its benefits outweigh its costs. That led to exceptions.

head: Exception
Case
Idea
rows: officers who reasonably relied on a warrant later found invalid; later cases extended the idea to other reasonable, good-faith mistakes
evidence also found through a separate lawful source
evidence police would have found anyway by lawful means
the link between the violation and the evidence is too weak

blocks.html: Evidence from unconstitutional searches is generally excluded: Weeks (1914) in federal court, Mapp (1961) in state courts. Exceptions: good faith (Leon), independent source, inevitable discovery (Nix) and attenuation. "Fruit of the poisonous tree" (evidence derived from the violation) is excluded too, unless an exception applies.

blocks.title: An invalid warrant
blocks.q: A judge issues a search warrant that a higher court later finds lacked probable cause. The officers had no reason to doubt it. Is the evidence excluded?
steps: The search violated the Fourth Amendment because the warrant was invalid.
But under United States v. Leon, officers who reasonably relied on a warrant act in good faith, and excluding evidence would not deter police misconduct.
blocks.a: No; the good-faith exception applies.

blocks.title: Search party
blocks.q: Police learn where evidence is through an unlawful interrogation, but a large search party already combing that area would have found it within hours. Admissible?
steps: The evidence is fruit of a violation.
Nix v. Williams: if the government proves it would inevitably have been found by lawful means, it is admissible.
blocks.a: Yes; inevitable discovery.

blocks.html: Thinking an illegal search ends the case. Only the tainted evidence is excluded, the prosecution may go on with other evidence, and the exceptions often let the evidence in. The rule also does not apply in some settings, such as grand juries and civil cases.

The Fifth Amendment says no person "shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself." Police questioning in a closed room can pressure people to speak. In 1966 the Court created a rule to protect the privilege during questioning. It applies in state cases through incorporation (Malloy v. Hogan, 1964) and works alongside the exclusionary rule.

opts.facts: Ernesto Miranda was arrested in Phoenix and questioned for about two hours without being told of his rights. He signed a confession. The Court decided his case with three others raising the same issue.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Warren wrote that custodial interrogation is inherently compelling. Before questioning a person in custody, police must warn that he has the right to remain silent, that anything he says can be used against him in court, that he has the right to the presence of a lawyer, and that if he cannot afford one, one will be appointed. Statements taken without the warnings and a valid waiver are generally inadmissible to prove guilt.
opts.dissent: Four justices dissented, arguing that the Court was writing a code of police procedure that the Constitution does not require and that would reduce confessions.

blocks.name: cv-order

items: The person knowingly and voluntarily waives the rights
If the person asks for a lawyer, questioning stops

blocks.cap: The Miranda sequence. Put it in order.

blocks.html: Miranda applies only to custodial interrogation: both parts must be present. Custody means a formal arrest or restraint like one; a routine traffic stop ordinarily is not custody. Interrogation means express questioning or its functional equivalent, words or actions police should know are reasonably likely to draw an incriminating response (Rhode Island v. Innis, 1980). Volunteered statements are not covered. There are limits. In New York v. Quarles (1984) the Court allowed a question about where a gun was hidden in a store before warnings, under a public safety exception. A suspect who wants to stop must say so clearly (Berghuis v. Thompkins, 2010). And in Dickerson v. United States (2000), 7 to 2, the Court held that Miranda is a constitutional rule that Congress could not overrule by a 1968 statute making voluntariness the only test.

Before custodial interrogation, police must give the Miranda warnings (silence; statements used in court; a lawyer; one appointed if needed). Both custody and interrogation are required. Dickerson (2000): Miranda is a constitutional rule Congress cannot overrule by statute.

blocks.title: A street conversation
blocks.q: An officer walking a beat asks a man on the sidewalk, who is free to leave, whether he saw what happened at a store. The man says he did it. Miranda violation?
steps: There is questioning, but no custody: the man was free to leave and not under arrest.
Miranda applies only to custodial interrogation.
blocks.a: No; the statement is admissible.

blocks.title: A blurted statement
blocks.q: After an arrest, and before any questions, a suspect in the back of the patrol car says, "I knew I should not have taken the money." Admissible?
steps: There is custody, but no interrogation: the officers asked nothing and did nothing designed to draw a statement.
Volunteered statements are not covered by Miranda.
blocks.a: Yes; it was volunteered.

blocks.html: Thinking Miranda applies whenever police speak with someone. It applies to custodial interrogation: both custody and questioning are required. Another slip: thinking a Miranda violation ends the case. Only the statements (and in some cases what they lead to) are excluded; other evidence remains.

The Fifth Amendment holds several protections in one sentence: grand juries for federal felony charges, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, due process and just compensation. This topic covers two: the privilege against self-incrimination (beyond the Miranda setting) and double jeopardy.

doc.title: The Fifth Amendment (excerpt)
paras: …nor shall any person be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb; nor shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself…

marks.note: The Double Jeopardy Clause (applied to the states in Benton v. Maryland, 1969).

marks.text: compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself
marks.note: The Self-Incrimination Clause (applied to the states in Malloy v. Hogan, 1964).

blocks.html: Self-incrimination. The privilege protects against compelled testimonial communications: being forced to reveal, by words, what is in one's mind. It does not cover physical evidence. In Schmerber v. California (1966) a blood sample taken from a driver was not testimony; the same is true of fingerprints, photographs, lineups and handwriting samples. A defendant may refuse to testify at trial, and the prosecutor may not comment on that silence to the jury (Griffin v. California, 1965). The government can compel testimony by granting immunity that covers both the testimony and evidence derived from it. Double jeopardy. A person may not be tried again for the same offense after an acquittal or conviction, or punished twice for it. "Same offense" is defined by the Blockburger test (1932): two crimes are different if each requires proof of a fact the other does not. A retrial after a hung jury is allowed, and so is a retrial after a defendant wins an appeal on trial errors.

opts.facts: Terance Gamble, who had a prior conviction, was stopped in Alabama and found with a handgun. Alabama prosecuted him for possessing it as a felon; then the federal government prosecuted him for the same possession under federal law.
opts.reasoning: Justice Alito wrote that an "offence" is defined by a sovereign's law, so a crime under state law and a crime under federal law are not the "same offence," even for the same act. The Court kept the long-standing separate-sovereigns doctrine.
opts.dissent: Justices Ginsburg and Gorsuch dissented, arguing that the doctrine lets two governments do together what neither could do alone.

blocks.html: The privilege covers compelled testimonial evidence, not physical evidence such as blood or fingerprints (Schmerber). Double jeopardy bars a second prosecution or punishment for the same offense (Blockburger test) by the same sovereign; state and federal governments may each prosecute (Gamble, 2019).

blocks.title: Same offense?
blocks.q: A driver is convicted of reckless driving (requires recklessness, not injury). Later the same state charges him with assault with a vehicle for the same incident (requires injury, not recklessness alone). Barred by Blockburger?
steps: Each crime requires proof of a fact the other does not: reckless driving needs recklessness; the assault charge needs injury.
Under Blockburger, they are different offenses.
blocks.a: Not barred under the Blockburger test (other doctrines, like collateral estoppel, could still matter).

blocks.title: Testimony or not?
blocks.q: Which is protected by the privilege: (a) being forced to give a voice sample, or (b) being forced to tell the jury where you were that night?
steps: A voice sample is physical, like a blood sample or handwriting: not testimonial.
Telling where you were reveals the contents of your mind: testimonial.
blocks.a: (b) is protected; (a) is not.

blocks.html: Thinking the privilege covers physical evidence such as fingerprints or blood samples. It protects testimonial communication, not physical evidence. Another slip: thinking double jeopardy bars a federal trial after a state trial. Separate sovereigns may each prosecute (Gamble).

The Sixth Amendment says "In all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall enjoy… the Assistance of Counsel for his defence." At first that meant a right to hire a lawyer. The question in the 1900s was whether government must provide one to people who cannot pay. It was decided case by case, through due process and then incorporation.

opts.facts: Clarence Earl Gideon was charged in Florida with breaking and entering a pool hall, a felony. He asked for a lawyer and was refused, because Florida appointed counsel only in capital cases. He defended himself, was convicted, and wrote a petition to the Supreme Court by hand from prison.
opts.reasoning: Justice Black wrote for a unanimous Court that "lawyers in criminal courts are necessities, not luxuries," and that the right to counsel is fundamental and binds the states. Betts v. Brady (1942), which had required counsel only in "special circumstances," was overruled.
opts.later: On retrial with a lawyer, Gideon was acquitted.

blocks.html: Gideon built on Powell v. Alabama (1932), in which the Court held that the young defendants in the Scottsboro case, tried for their lives in Alabama without real help from a lawyer, were denied due process. Later cases set the reach of the right: no one may be imprisoned for any offense, even a misdemeanor, without counsel (Argersinger v. Hamlin (1972)), but where only a fine is imposed, counsel is not required (Scott v. Illinois (1979)). The right covers critical stages before trial and a first appeal. Effective help matters too. Under Strickland v. Washington (1984), a defendant claiming ineffective assistance must show (1) deficient performance, below an objective standard of reasonableness, judged without hindsight and with a strong presumption of competence; and (2) prejudice, a reasonable probability that but for the errors the result would have been different.

Powell v. Alabama (1932) required counsel in a capital case like Scottsboro; Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), overruling Betts, required states to provide counsel to poor defendants charged with felonies; Argersinger extended it to any case that results in imprisonment. Strickland: ineffective assistance needs deficient performance and prejudice.

blocks.title: A misdemeanor
blocks.q: A defendant who cannot afford a lawyer is charged with a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months in jail. The judge refuses to appoint counsel and sentences him to 30 days. Valid?
steps: Gideon covered felonies; Argersinger (1972) extended the right to any case in which the defendant is actually imprisoned.
He was sentenced to jail without counsel.
blocks.a: Invalid; the jail sentence cannot stand without counsel.

blocks.title: Strickland
blocks.q: A lawyer failed to object to a piece of evidence, but the rest of the evidence of guilt was overwhelming. Does the defendant win an ineffective assistance claim?
steps: Even if failing to object was deficient performance, Strickland also requires prejudice.
With overwhelming other evidence, there is no reasonable probability of a different result.
blocks.a: No; prejudice is missing.

blocks.html: Thinking Gideon required lawyers in every case. It covered felonies; Argersinger (1972) and later cases extended it to misdemeanors that result in imprisonment. Where only a fine is imposed, appointed counsel is not constitutionally required (Scott v. Illinois).

The Sixth Amendment also promises "a speedy and public trial, by an impartial jury" and the right "to be confronted with the witnesses against him." These rights shape every criminal trial, and several were applied to the states through incorporation. This topic follows the right to counsel.

head: Right
Case
Rule
rows: any offense punishable by more than six months; petty offenses may be tried by a judge
six-person juries allowed in state cases
a unanimous verdict is required to convict of a serious offense in state court; overruled Apodaca (1972)
a prosecutor may not strike jurors because of their race (and, later, sex: J.E.B. v. Alabama, 1994)
testimonial statements of a witness who does not testify are barred unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior chance to cross-examine

opts.facts: Michael Crawford was tried for stabbing a man. The prosecution played a recorded statement his wife had given to police. She did not testify at trial because of the state's marital privilege, so Crawford could not cross-examine her.
opts.reasoning: Justice Scalia wrote that the Confrontation Clause, read in light of its history (including abuses like the trial of Sir Walter Raleigh), demands that testimonial statements be tested by cross-examination. Reliability as judged by a court is not a substitute. Ohio v. Roberts (1980) was set aside for testimonial statements.

blocks.html: What is testimonial? Statements made mainly to establish past facts for a prosecution, such as formal police interrogations or forensic lab reports prepared for trial (Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts, 2009). A 911 call made to get help in an ongoing emergency is not testimonial (Davis v. Washington, 2006). Batson created a three-step process: the defendant shows a prima facie case that a strike was based on race; the prosecutor gives a race-neutral reason; the judge decides whether the reason is a pretext. In Ramos the majority (Justice Gorsuch) relied on the historical meaning of "trial by jury"; the dissent stressed stare decisis and reliance on Apodaca by two states.

Duncan v. Louisiana (1968) incorporated the jury right for serious crimes (over six months, Baldwin); Ramos v. Louisiana (2020) requires unanimous state felony juries; Batson v. Kentucky (1986) bars race-based strikes; Crawford v. Washington (2004) requires cross-examination for testimonial statements.

blocks.title: A petty offense
blocks.q: A defendant charged with a crime punishable by at most 90 days in jail asks for a jury. Must the state provide one?
steps: Under Baldwin, offenses punishable by six months or less are presumptively petty.
90 days is under six months.
blocks.a: No jury is constitutionally required.

blocks.title: A lab report
blocks.q: At a drug trial, the prosecution offers a sworn lab certificate saying the substance is cocaine, without calling the analyst. Objection?
steps: The certificate was made to prove a fact at trial: testimonial.
Melendez-Diaz (2009), applying Crawford, requires the analyst to be available for cross-examination.
blocks.a: The objection should be sustained under the Confrontation Clause.

blocks.html: Thinking the Sixth Amendment guarantees a jury in every criminal case. It applies to serious offenses; petty offenses (generally six months or less) may be tried without a jury.

doc.title: The Eighth Amendment
paras: Excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted.

marks.note: Bail set higher than needed to assure that the accused will appear.
Most cases concern the death penalty and long sentences.

blocks.html: The Eighth Amendment closes the criminal procedure unit, after juries and confrontation. It governs what happens after conviction, and before trial for bail.

The death penalty. In Furman v. Georgia (1972), a short per curiam opinion, five justices held that death sentences as then imposed were unconstitutional; each of the nine wrote separately. Two (Brennan and Marshall) would have held the penalty always unconstitutional; three objected to how arbitrarily it was applied. States rewrote their laws, and in Gregg v. Georgia (1976) the Court upheld Georgia's new system: a separate sentencing phase, guidance for juries about aggravating and mitigating factors, and appellate review. Mandatory death sentences were struck down the same day (Woodson v. North Carolina, 1976). The Court has since placed categorical limits, asking about "evolving standards of decency" (a phrase from Trop v. Dulles, 1958) as shown by state laws and practice: no death penalty for people with intellectual disabilities (Atkins v. Virginia (2002)), for people under 18 at the time of the crime (Roper v. Simmons (2005)), or for crimes against individuals that did not take a life (Kennedy v. Louisiana (2008)). Justices who read the clause by its original meaning, such as Justices Scalia and Thomas, have argued that it bars only punishments considered cruel and unusual when adopted, and have dissented from some of these limits; others defend the evolving-standards approach. Fines. In Timbs v. Indiana (2019) Indiana sought to forfeit a man's Land Rover, worth about four times the maximum fine for his drug crime. The Court unanimously held that the Excessive Fines Clause applies to the states.

The Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail and fines and cruel and unusual punishments. Furman v. Georgia (1972) halted death sentences under existing laws; Gregg v. Georgia (1976) upheld revised procedures; the Court has barred the death penalty for people with intellectual disabilities (Atkins) and for those under 18 at the crime (Roper); Timbs v. Indiana (2019) incorporated the Excessive Fines Clause.

blocks.title: Age at the time of the crime
blocks.q: A man committed a murder at 17 and is tried at 20. May the state seek the death penalty?
steps: Roper v. Simmons (2005) bars the death penalty for crimes committed under 18.
What counts is age at the time of the crime, not at trial.
blocks.a: No.

blocks.title: Furman's effect
blocks.q: Did Furman v. Georgia abolish the death penalty?
steps: Furman struck down death sentences as then imposed, mainly because of arbitrary application.
Only two justices would have held the penalty always unconstitutional.
Four years later, Gregg upheld revised statutes.
blocks.a: No; it struck down the systems then in use, and Gregg upheld revised ones.

blocks.html: Thinking Furman abolished the death penalty. It struck down the way it was then imposed; Gregg upheld revised statutes four years later. Many states and the federal government have the death penalty today, and many states have abolished it by law.

The Fifth Amendment ends: "nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation." It was the clause at issue in Barron (1833), and it reached the states in Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Co. v. Chicago (1897). It does not forbid taking property; it sets two conditions: the taking must be for a public use, and the owner must be paid just compensation (usually fair market value). Economic regulation otherwise gets rational basis review; the Takings Clause is a separate check.

opts.facts: New London, Connecticut, a city with a struggling economy, adopted a development plan for the Fort Trumbull area near a new research facility, with offices, housing and a riverwalk. Susette Kelo and other owners who refused to sell, whose homes were not blighted, challenged the use of eminent domain.
opts.reasoning: Justice Stevens wrote that the Court has long read "public use" as "public purpose," deferring to legislative judgments (Berman v. Parker, Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff). A carefully considered economic development plan serves a public purpose even though the land passes to private developers. Compensation was required and was not in dispute.
opts.dissent: Justice O'Connor (joined by three) said that under this reading nothing prevents the state from transferring any property to a private owner who would use it more productively. Justice Thomas argued for returning to the original meaning: use by the public.
opts.later: Many states then passed laws or amendments limiting the use of eminent domain for economic development.

blocks.html: Regulatory takings. Government can also take property without seizing it, by regulating it heavily. In Pennsylvania Coal Co. v. Mahon (1922) Justice Holmes wrote that "if regulation goes too far it will be recognized as a taking." How far is too far?

head: Rule
Case
When
rows: Physical occupation is a taking, however small
a permanent physical occupation (a cable box on a roof)
Total loss of economic value is a taking
a rule leaves land with no economically beneficial use, unless background principles of property or nuisance law already forbade the use
Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City (1978)
weigh the economic impact, interference with distinct investment-backed expectations, and the character of the government action

blocks.html: In Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City (1978) New York's landmarks law blocked a tower above Grand Central Terminal; the owner could still use the terminal profitably and could transfer its development rights, so there was no taking. In Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council (1992) a coastal law barred building on two beachfront lots bought for homes, leaving them without economic use; that was a taking unless state property law already forbade such building. Conditions on building permits (exactions) must have an essential nexus and rough proportionality to the project's impacts (Nollan v. California Coastal Commission, 1987, and later cases).

Takings: property may be taken only for public use with just compensation. Kelo v. City of New London (2005), 5 to 4, held economic development a public use. Regulations are takings if they cause a permanent physical occupation (Loretto), a total loss of economic value (Lucas), or go "too far" under Penn Central balancing.

blocks.title: Which test?
blocks.q: A town rezones a lot so that the owner can build only one house instead of the four she planned; the lot loses 40 percent of its value. Taking?
steps: No physical occupation, and not a total loss of value.
So Penn Central balancing applies: a 40 percent loss, her expectations, and the character of a general zoning law.
Courts usually find no taking in cases like this.
blocks.a: Penn Central balancing; likely not a taking.

blocks.title: A tiny box
blocks.q: A city requires apartment owners to let a utility install a small box on their roofs, permanently, without payment. Taking?
steps: A permanent physical occupation of property.
Loretto: that is a taking regardless of size or public benefit.
Just compensation is owed (it may be small).
blocks.a: Yes; compensation is owed.

blocks.html: Thinking Kelo let governments take property without paying. Compensation was required; the question was whether the taking was for a "public use." Many states narrowed eminent domain after Kelo by statute or constitutional amendment.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) says the right to vote shall not be denied or abridged "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude," and gives Congress power to enforce it. For nearly a century, many states got around it with literacy tests, poll taxes and intimidation. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 (VRA) was Congress's answer. This topic builds on fundamental rights and on Congress's enforcement powers.

head: Part of the VRA
What it does
Status
rows: nationwide: bars any voting practice that results in denying or abridging the right to vote on account of race (a "results" test since the 1982 amendments)
in force; applied in Thornburg v. Gingles (1986)
the coverage formula: which states and counties were covered, based on tests and turnout data
struck down in Shelby County v. Holder (2013)
covered places had to get federal approval ("preclearance") before changing voting rules
not struck down, but has no effect without a coverage formula

opts.facts: Shelby County, Alabama, a covered jurisdiction, sued, arguing that the coverage formula, last updated with data from the 1960s and 1970s and reauthorized in 2006 for 25 years, was unconstitutional.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts wrote that the formula was justified in 1965 but rested on decades-old data and eradicated practices, while departing from the principle that states have equal sovereignty. Congress could draft a new formula based on current conditions. The Court did not rule on Section 5 itself.
opts.dissent: Justice Ginsburg (joined by three) argued that Congress had built a large record in 2006, that preclearance was a main reason discrimination in voting had fallen, and that Congress was entitled to keep it.

blocks.html: Section 2 today. In Thornburg v. Gingles (1986) the Court set three preconditions for a vote dilution claim: the minority group is large and geographically compact enough to form a majority in a district; it is politically cohesive; and the majority usually votes as a bloc to defeat its preferred candidates. Courts then look at the totality of circumstances. In 2026 the Court narrowed how Section 2 applies to redistricting. Two kinds of gerrymandering claims. Racial gerrymandering, drawing districts mainly by race, is subject to strict scrutiny under equal protection (Shaw v. Reno (1993)), and vote dilution claims arise under Section 2. But in Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) the Court held 5 to 4 that claims of partisan gerrymandering present political questions beyond the reach of federal courts; the Chief Justice noted that state courts, state constitutions and Congress may address them. Justice Kagan's dissent argued courts could manage such claims.

Section 2 of the VRA bars voting practices that result in denying or abridging the vote on account of race; Thornburg v. Gingles (1986) set the preconditions for vote dilution claims. Shelby County v. Holder (2013) struck down the preclearance coverage formula. Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) left partisan gerrymandering claims to the political process and state courts.

blocks.title: Which claim?
blocks.q: Voters say their state's legislature drew congressional districts to help one party win more seats. Can a federal court hear the claim?
steps: This is a partisan gerrymandering claim.
Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) held such claims are political questions for federal courts.
Voters may pursue claims under a state constitution in state court, or ask Congress or the state to act.
blocks.a: Not in federal court after Rucho.

blocks.title: Section 5 after Shelby
blocks.q: After Shelby County, must Alabama get federal approval before changing its voting rules?
steps: Shelby struck down Section 4(b), the formula that decided who was covered.
Section 5 still exists but covers no one without a formula.
Section 2 still applies nationwide, through lawsuits.
blocks.a: No; preclearance has no effect without a coverage formula, though Section 2 suits remain.

blocks.html: Mixing up racial and partisan gerrymandering claims. Racial claims can be heard in federal court under the Constitution (Shaw) and the VRA (Gingles); after Rucho, purely partisan claims cannot.
